title: How to Build a Simple AI Model Router
content:
If every request in your app goes to your biggest AI model, you are probably paying for power you don't need.
Here is how to build a simple model router.
This is a build walkthrough, step by step.
The idea is simple.
Some questions are easy, like "What are your opening hours?"
Some are hard, like "Compare these two contracts and flag the risks."
A router sends each question to the right model.
Step ONE. Define two lanes.
A fast, cheap model for simple tasks.
And a stronger model for reasoning, long documents and anything high stakes.
Two lanes is enough to start. Don't build ten.
Step TWO. Classify the request before you answer it.
Start with plain rules. Length of the input, keywords, whether files are attached.
Later, you can use a small model to label each request as easy or hard.
The classifier must be much cheaper than the work it saves.
Now, the step most people skip.
And it is the one that keeps your router honest.
Step THREE. Add a fallback.
If the fast model's answer fails a check, send the same request to the strong model.
A check can be simple. Is the format valid? Did it cite a source? Did it refuse?
Users should never pay for a bad routing decision.
Step FOUR. Log everything.
Which lane, how long it took, what it cost, and whether the answer was correct.
Then review a sample every week and move the line between easy and hard.
Many providers now offer OpenAI-compatible APIs, so switching models is often just a change of model name and endpoint.
That makes routing much easier to try than it used to be.
Here's my take. Don't trust anyone's savings number, including mine.
Measure cost and accuracy on your own traffic, before and after.
That before-and-after table is also a great story for any AI engineering interview.
